rationale: B wins because it has better PR judgment, not because A is weak. B's "A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product" is an ownable business-model story with hard proof attached, while A's "Deel's new AI compliance tool arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage" is newsworthy but asks Deel to pitch its own reputational problem. A's accuracy angle is solid, but B's line that the lawsuit is "a question every reporter will ask, not an angle the company can own" is the adult supervision here.
gaps_in_A: "Deel's new AI compliance tool arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage" is a real reporter story, but a dangerous company-led pitch. It treats reputational exposure as an angle Deel can sell, not mainly a prep burden.
"a budget question for HR teams' outside counsel" is plausible but speculative. No outside-counsel spend, customer substitution, or legal-review behavior is in the supplied facts.
"24hr" decay on the accuracy-disclosure angle undersells the story. Liability around undisclosed accuracy in legal-adjacent AI can live longer than launch day.
The next step says to "try to close those gaps directly with Deel," which is awkward if this is meant to advise Deel. Say exactly which proof Deel must produce before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "automating that call" overstates the facts. The update says the tool checks and flags risks; it does not say Deel makes final legal determinations.

"Perspective lens, regulator-and-rules protagonist" drags in a regulator frame without a supplied regulator signal. The copy later admits none exists, so keep the protagonist as employer liability or legal risk.
"One employer, one bad contractor call" is useful only as a proof hunt. Without a named customer and real flag, it is not a pitchable angle yet.
"meanest-editor on the pricing angle" is a slightly odd next step. The immediate move is to get the executive pricing rationale and then run journalist fit, not workshop the angle again.
